During the first 0.02-0.03s of ventricular contraction, the pressure in the atria is higher than in the ventricles so the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) are open. However, as the pressure in the ventricles rises above that in the atria, the atrioventricular valves shut causing back pressure and so preventing any flow from the atria into the ventricles. At the same time, the pressure in the aorta and pulmonary trunk is higher than in the ventricles so the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) are closed. As the ventricles contract, there is little shortening of muscle fibers because the pressure is building up so the volume doesn't decrease. This period is called isovolumetric contraction and it occurs just before S1 heart sound which is when the first valve closure occurs. The total duration of this phase is 0.02-0.03s whereas passive filling of the ventricles lasts 0.06-0.1s (diastole) which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers but the volume increases. This period is called isovolumetric diastole and it occurs just before S2 heart sound which is when the second set of valves shut.

Simple squamous- this is the correct answer, these cells are one cell thick with a flat outline shape. They are found in the alveoli, Bowman's capsule in the kidneys and the lining of some blood vessels. Them thin structure makes them ideal for filtration and diffusion.  Simple cuboidal- these are one cell thick with a cube shape. They are found in the kidney tubules and the ducts and small tubes of some glands. Properties similar to simple squamous however not as thin so isn't as ideal for filtration and diffusion. Rough (with rER) and smooth (without e.R) versions exist. Simple columnar- this is two to multiple cell thick with a column shape. They are found in the digestive tract and some glands. Can have microvilli on their top surface to increase absorption (absorptive epithelium) or cilia for movement of mucus (motor epithelium) Pseudostratified- these are multiple but not uniform in height giving the appearance of multiple layers. Found in the trachea and upper respiratory tract. Ciliated version for movement of mucus and non-ciliated (with keratin) version for strength and protection. Stratified squamous- this is thick, multiple layer cells with a flat shape. They are found in the oesophagus, vagina, urethra, anus, external lips and in the mouth. Non-keratinised version is found in moist areas like the mouth and is mainly for protection keratinised version is found in areas that need protection from abrasion e.g. fingertips

Haemochromatosis is a disorder characterised by a mutation in the gene that regulates the production of hepcidin (or its reduced absorption), a peptide that controls levels of the iron hormone ferritin in the blood. Low levels of the active form of the peptide, hepcidin, means that iron is not properly regulated and accumulates in the body, particularly in the liver, heart and the reproductive glands.

The correct answer is A - selectins are proteins used by the immune system to help white blood cells roll along the inside of blood vessels during inflammation. They are found on the surface of the leukocytes and the endothelial surfaces that line the blood vessels. Integrins are also found on the surface of leukocytes and are important for the adhesion of the white blood cell to the vessel wall. However, they are not involved in the rolling process. Some integrins are activated by chemokines which stimulate firm adhesion - this is an important step in the migration process. PECAM-1 (also known as CD31) is a transmembrane protein found mainly as a junction protein in endothelial cells. It is important in transmigration. Some areas where it is found include the blood-brain barrier and the barrier formed by endothelial cells in inflammation. Fibrin is a cytoskeletal protein in the immune system used in the body's clotting cascade. It is not involved in the migration of white blood cells. Keratin is a cytoskeletal protein found in epithelial cells. It is not involved in the migration of white blood cells. For more information I found case 5 in immunology and inflammation is helpful.
